fact: Almost half the wood in it is dead — ten times a managed forest — and half of its 12,000 species need the rotting logs.

name: Amsterdam Canal Ring
fact: Three concentric canals dug in one plan in the 17th century, and the city has been the shape of that plan ever since.

name: Lock (canal)
fact: A boat lift with no machinery. Shut both gates, let water in or out, and the boat rides up or down on it.

name: Panama Canal
fact: Not a cut through the isthmus but a staircase over it: ships are lifted 26 m to a lake and let down the other side.

name: Great Stupa at Sanchi
fact: A brick dome over relics, later doubled in size and cased in stone. The gateways came two centuries after the building.

name: Kalyan Minaret
fact: Fired brick in gypsum mortar, 45.6 m of it, standing since 1127. Genghis Khan had it spared while the city around it came down.

name: Cité de Carcassonne
fact: Two concentric walls and 52 towers — and a 19th-century restoration that roofed it in slate from a region with no slate in it.

name: Rila Monastery
fact: Burned to the ground in 1833 and rebuilt by public subscription — striped arcades, 300 chambers, and frescoes finished in 1846.

name: Sungbo's Eredo
fact: More than 160 km of ditch and bank in laterite, ringing a kingdom, with 20 m from ditch floor to bank rim.

name: Volcanic Ash
fact: Not smoke — rock. Magma torn into fragments under 2 mm across, which is why it settles as a blanket and stays where it lands.

name: Joya de Cerén
fact: A Maya farming village under ten metres of ash, with the crops still in the ground and nobody in the houses. They had time to leave.

name: Monte Albán
fact: A mountain top flattened by hand, 400 m above the valley and 500 years before Christ, then built on for a millennium.

name: Fasil Ghebbi
fact: Brown basalt trimmed in wine-coloured tuff — Portuguese, Indian and Arab building put together by Ethiopian emperors behind one wall.

name: Bikini Atoll
fact: Twenty-three devices, about 77 megatons, and a fleet on the lagoon floor. Listed by UNESCO for exactly that.

name: Levuka
fact: Fiji’s first colonial capital, kept as it was because the hills behind it left no room to grow and the government left instead.

name: Sangha Trinational
fact: One forest, three countries, and the clearings in it — the bais — are where the elephants can be counted at all.

name: Pantheon
fact: Still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, nineteen centuries on. It gets lighter as it goes up, on purpose.

name: Parthenon
fact: Almost nothing in it is straight. The floor bulges 10.3 cm over 70 m and the columns lean inward, so that it looks straight.

name: Knossos
fact: Lit from above rather than from the sides, so rooms deep inside a dense building still get daylight and air.

name: Meteora
fact: Twenty-four monasteries on top of conglomerate pillars, reached for three centuries only by rope, basket and removable ladder.

name: Pompeii
fact: The bodies rotted and left holes. Fiorelli poured plaster into the holes, and got the people back.

name: Mount Etna
fact: Its own height is not a fixed number: 3,403 m in September 2024, and it changes with every summit eruption.

name: Dome of the Rock
fact: An octagon built around one rock, finished in 691–2. The dome is wooden, and the one standing now replaced the original after it fell in 1015.

name: Masada
fact: A desert plateau made habitable by cisterns holding 40,000 m³ — and taken in the end by a ramp 114 m high.

name: Cappadocia
fact: Soft volcanic rock under a hard cap: the cap protects a column while everything around it goes, and then people cut houses into what is left.

name: Grand Canyon
fact: 446 km long and over 1,850 m deep, cut in about five million years through rock two billion years old.

name: Salar de Uyuni
fact: 10,582 km² of salt whose elevation varies by less than a metre — flat enough that satellites are calibrated against it.

name: Urnes Stave Church
fact: Standing on staves rather than sills, from about 1132 — and carved on the north portal in the last Viking animal style.

name: Harappa
fact: 23,500 people in flat-roofed brick houses on a near-orthogonal plan, with drains. Then the Lahore–Multan railway used it for ballast.

name: Hoover Dam
fact: Poured in blocks with 937 km of pipe inside them, because left to itself the concrete would have taken 125 years to cool.

name: Grand Canal
fact: 1,776 km of canal with a summit 42 m up, and the pound lock — invented for it in 984 — is what let boats get over the top.

name: Suomenlinna
fact: A star fort bent onto six rocky islands, called the Gibraltar of the North, surrendered after two months.

name: Tōdai-ji
fact: 500 tonnes of bronze inside what was, until 1998, the largest wooden building in the world — and the hall is 30% smaller than the one before it.

name: Qhapaq Ñan
fact: About 40,000 km of road with no wheel on it anywhere, and fibre bridges that had to be rebuilt every two years.

name: Cologne Cathedral
fact: Begun 1248, abandoned around 1560, finished in 1880 to the medieval drawings that had survived the gap — 632 years, and it was the tallest building on Earth for four of them.

name: Notre-Dame de Paris
fact: The weight of the roof is carried outside the building, which is what lets the walls be thin and the windows large. The roof itself burned in 2019.

name: Yellowstone
fact: The first national park, and the reason it is worth protecting is a magma chamber: at least 1,283 geysers and 10,000 hydrothermal features over one caldera.

name: Iguazu Falls
fact: Three layers of basalt make a two-step staircase 2.7 km wide, and about half the river goes down one throat in it.

name: Angel Falls
fact: A plunge of 807 m off the edge of a table mountain — far enough that in the dry season the water is mist before it lands.

name: Seokguram
fact: An artificial granite dome assembled with stone rivets and no mortar, which let it breathe — until a concrete restoration stopped it.

name: Port Arthur
fact: A prison whose outer wall is the sea. The only way off the peninsula was a 30-metre neck, fenced, and lined with dogs.

name: Kakadu Rock Art
fact: More than 5,000 recorded sites, some paintings up to 20,000 years old, on ground occupied continuously for around 60,000.

name: Tash Rabat
fact: Thirty-one domed stone rooms at 3,200 m, each lit through a hole at the top of its own dome.

name: Larabanga Mosque
fact: Eight metres square, twelve conical buttresses, and timbers laid through the walls — adobe needs help, and this is what the help looks like.

name: Volubilis
fact: Fifty-eight olive-pressing complexes in one Roman town, and its stone later went into Meknes.

name: Ayutthaya
fact: A capital on an island made by three rivers, which is a moat you do not have to dig — until a siege lasts fourteen months.

name: Baalbek
fact: The largest ancient block known is still lying in the quarry: 19.6 m long and an estimated 1,650 tonnes, never moved.

name: Aral Sea
fact: The fourth-largest lake on Earth in 1960, and a tenth of that by 2007. Nothing was done to the lake — the work was all done to the two rivers.

name: Sagrada Família
fact: Gaudí found his arches by hanging weighted strings upside down: a chain in tension, inverted, is a line in pure compression.

name: Hwaseong Fortress
fact: Built 1794–96 with pulleys and paid labour, and written up afterwards in ten volumes — including the wages.

name: Sundarbans
fact: A forest standing in salt and airless mud, breathing through roots that grow upward — and a sea wall for millions of people.

name: Cueva de las Manos
fact: Over 2,000 hands, 829 left to 31 right — because you hold the pipe in the hand you are better with and stencil the other one.

name: Palenque
fact: A city with mains water: a corbel-vaulted conduit over 100 m long, run under the main plaza to put a stream where the builders wanted it.

name: Palmyra
fact: A city that exists because of one spring in the desert, and got rich on the caravans that had to stop at it.

name: Aachen Cathedral
fact: Charlemagne’s chapel, built about 796 partly out of columns shipped from Rome and Ravenna — the empire assembled from pieces of the last one.

name: Moscow Kremlin
fact: Oak, then white limestone, then 2,235 m of brick wall put up by Italians between 1485 and 1495.

name: Mauna Kea
fact: 4,207 m above the sea and 9,330 m above its own base — and its summit sits above the inversion layer, which is why the telescopes are there.

name: Palace of Versailles
fact: 2,143 windows, 1,252 chimneys and 67 staircases: a palace built so a whole court could be watched living in one building.

name: Unfinished Obelisk
fact: Nearly 1,090 tonnes, a third larger than any obelisk ever raised — and still attached to the quarry floor, because it cracked.

name: Nok Terracotta
fact: Near life-size hollow heads, coil-built and burnished, fired under a heap of grass and twigs. The eyes are pierced, which is how they survived the firing.

name: Igbo-Ukwu Bronzes
fact: Lost-wax castings of ninth-century Nigeria, buried with more than 150,000 glass beads that came from Egypt and Mesopotamia.

name: Mount Kilimanjaro
fact: The highest free-standing mountain in the world, and its ice cover fell from 11.40 km² to under 1 between 1912 and 2011.

name: Niagara Falls
fact: The falls are moving upstream: hard caprock over soft shale, undercut until the cap breaks off. Diversion for power has slowed it to about 30 cm a year.

name: Mỹ Sơn
fact: Cham temples of fired brick with the ornament carved into the brick itself, and no organic trace of mortar between the courses.

name: Tassili n'Ajjer
fact: Fifteen thousand engravings of antelope, crocodile and cattle herds — in the middle of the Sahara, because it was not one.

name: Temple of the Oracle, Siwa
fact: Built of kershif — salt and mud — and palm logs, which is fine in a place with no rain until it rains for three days.

name: Djémila
fact: A Roman grid laid on a narrow triangular ridge at 900 m, where the ground was so tight the theatre had to go outside the walls.

name: Cape Coast Castle
fact: Swedish, then Danish, then Dutch, then English — and dungeons cut into the rock beneath the parade ground that could hold a thousand people.

name: Manhyia Palace
fact: Built by the British in 1925 to house the king they had exiled — and he would not take it until he had paid for it in full.

name: Drakensberg Rock Art
fact: Between 35,000 and 40,000 San works, the largest such collection anywhere, painted on soft sandstone under a hard basalt cap.

name: Lamu Old Town
fact: Built of the reef and the swamp — coral rag walls on mangrove poles — and still worked by about 3,000 donkeys, because the streets were never sized for anything else.

name: Dzanga-Sangha
fact: Forest elephants gather in one clearing to eat the mineral soil, which is the only reason anyone has ever been able to watch them properly.

name: Loango
fact: A coastal kingdom that exported copper and cloth to Europe before it exported people, and outlived the trade that made it famous by only a few decades.

name: Tsodilo
fact: Four quartzite hills standing out of the Kalahari with over 4,500 paintings on them, and the San call it the birthplace of all life.

name: Old Quebec
fact: The only walled city north of Mexico, in two halves — one on top of a cliff and one at the bottom of it.

name: Copán
fact: A staircase of 62 steps carrying 2,200 glyphs — the longest Maya text there is, and it is a flight of stairs.

name: Red Fort
fact: A water channel called the River of Paradise runs through the palaces, so the cooling is part of the architecture rather than added to it.

name: Anuradhapura
fact: Capital for about 1,500 years, with brick stupas among the largest structures of the ancient world and a fig tree that has been documented since it was planted.

name: Kronborg
fact: Built where the Sound is only 4 km wide, so that a king could make every ship entering the Baltic pay him.

name: Geirangerfjord
fact: A glacier cut a valley below sea level and left; the sea came in. The farms on the cliffs above were reached by paths bolted to the rock.

name: Neuschwanstein
fact: A medieval fantasy with central heating, running hot water, flushing lavatories and telephone lines — and only about fifteen rooms ever finished.

name: Dead Sea
fact: 439.78 m below sea level and 9.6 times as salty as the ocean, because water arrives and only ever leaves as vapour.

name: Erdene Zuu
fact: Built in 1585 out of the stones of Karakorum, and destroyed in 1939 by a purge that killed more than ten thousand monks.

name: Hue Citadel
fact: European bastion geometry laid out for a Vietnamese emperor, nearly 10 km round with walls 21 m thick — and 150 of its 160 buildings were destroyed in 1968.

name: Sukhothai
fact: A city built around its ponds, and the 1292 inscription found in it is where written Thai starts.

name: Prague Castle
fact: The largest ancient castle in the world, almost 70,000 m², with a cathedral inside it that took six centuries to finish.

name: Waitangi Treaty Grounds
fact: The Treaty of New Zealand was signed in a marquee on a lawn on 6 February 1840, and the country has argued about the two texts of it ever since.

name: Haʻamonga ʻa Maui
fact: Three coral limestone slabs, the uprights 30 to 40 tonnes each, raised about 1200 AD on an island with no quarry stone but reef.

name: Otrar
fact: A caravan city that killed a caravan in 1218, and the war that answered it reached the Danube. Forty families were left by 1800.

name: Patan Durbar Square
fact: Newar brick and timber with 136 courtyards and 55 major temples, in a valley that keeps knocking them down.

name: Trogir
fact: A Greek grid from the 3rd century BC, still legible under everything Rome, Venice and the Middle Ages put on top of it.

name: Euphrasian Basilica
fact: The best-preserved early Christian church there is, standing on two older ones — the floor of the 5th-century basilica is still underneath it.

name: Sighișoara
fact: Each tower in the wall belonged to a guild and was maintained by it, so the defence of the town was divided up like its trades.

name: Te Wāhipounamu
fact: 2.6 million hectares named for the greenstone in it — the best surviving sample of what Gondwana looked like.

name: Auschwitz-Birkenau
fact: 1.1 million people were murdered here, 960,000 of them Jews. It is preserved as evidence, and it has been a museum since 2 July 1947.

name: Vigeland Installation
fact: 212 sculptures by one man, including a 14.12 m column of 121 figures cut from a single block by three masons over fourteen years.

name: East Rennell
fact: The largest raised coral atoll in the world: its lagoon is now a brackish lake sitting at sea level, on land that used to be underwater.

name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau
fact: A wall that made the ground inside it legally different: reach it after breaking a kapu and a priest could absolve you instead of the law killing you.

name: Morne Trois Pitons
fact: A flooded fumarole 82–92 °C at the edge and hotter in the middle, in a valley of boiling mud and small geysers.

name: Cueva de las Maravillas
fact: 472 Taíno paintings and about 10 engravings, 25 m underground in a limestone reef that used to be a reef.

name: Stale Bread
fact: Not dryness — the starch recrystallising. It happens fastest just above freezing, so a fridge stales bread quicker than the counter does.

name: Table Olive
fact: A raw olive is inedible. Curing takes the oleuropein out; the lactic acid that replaces it is also what lets the jar sit on a shelf.

name: Puff Pastry
fact: Nothing leavens it but the water in its own butter. Fold it right and eighty-one layers of steam lift it.

name: Wood-Tar Creosote
fact: The reason smoking preserves meat, isolated: about half of it is guaiacol and creosol. Reichenbach worked that out in 1832.

name: Abu Simbel
fact: Cut into a cliff so the sun reaches the back wall twice a year — then sawn into 1,036 blocks and moved 208 m inland and 65 m up.

name: Timbuktu
fact: Where salt from 664 km north met gold from the south, and the profit was spent on books — about 350,000 manuscripts have been got out.

name: Stone Town
fact: Built out of coral, rich on cloves and slaves, and the cathedral’s altar stands on the spot where the whipping post did.

name: Taos Pueblo
fact: Adobe several feet thick, stacked five or six storeys, lived in for about a thousand years — and no electricity or plumbing in the old village, by choice.

name: Uxmal
fact: Puuc building is a hut translated into stone: reeds become columns, a thatched roof becomes a trapezoid, and the pyramid is oval.

name: Chan Chan
fact: The largest adobe city in the Americas, standing because it almost never rains — and being lost now to the times it does.

name: Karnak
fact: 134 columns in 5,000 m², carrying architraves estimated at 70 tonnes, on a site built and rebuilt for about 1,900 years.

name: Bandiagara Escarpment
fact: A 500 m sandstone cliff with granaries and burials cut into it — put up high to keep them above the flash floods.

name: Virunga
fact: Africa’s first national park, 1925, and on the Danger list since 1994. 175 rangers were killed there up to April 2018.

name: Okavango Delta
fact: A delta that never reaches the sea. Its flood peaks in the dry winter, because the rain that makes it fell in Angola five months earlier.

name: Statue of Liberty
fact: A copper skin 2.4 mm thick hung on an iron frame designed to let it move — and it went green within twenty years, which is what protects it.

name: Cusco
fact: The 1650 earthquake destroyed almost every colonial building in it. The Inca walls underneath them are still there.

name: Valley of the Kings
fact: 65 tombs cut into rock that swells when it gets wet — which is why the flash floods that fill them also split them open.

name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
fact: One of the last sacred forests left around a Yoruba city, and its shrines were rebuilt as sculpture by an Austrian artist who stayed fifty years.

name: Lake Turkana
fact: The largest permanent desert lake and the largest alkaline lake on Earth, and the basin around it is where Turkana Boy and Skull 1470 came from.

name: Golden Gate Bridge
fact: Painted international orange because it had to be seen in fog. Each cable is 27,572 strands of wire.

name: Calakmul
fact: A city of 50,000 with 117 stelae, under rainforest — the Snake Kingdom, and Tikal’s opposite number for two centuries.

name: Torres del Paine
fact: Granite that never reached the surface until everything above it was taken away — first by weather, then by ice.

name: Simien Mountains
fact: Three kilometres of stacked lava, cut back into pinnacles and gorges — and one of the few places in tropical Africa where it snows.

name: Yosemite Valley
fact: A river cut a V and the ice widened it into a U, which is why the walls are vertical and the falls come off them.

name: Viñales Valley
fact: Limestone towers up to 300 m with tobacco grown by ox between them — the same karst shape as Guilin, on the other side of the world.

name: Itchan Kala
fact: 6,250 m of mud-brick wall around the last stop before the desert crossing, and a minaret so wide at the base that it was never finished.

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
fact: Carved to calm a dangerous confluence — and it worked, because the spoil went into the river and changed the current.

name: Hampi
fact: The second-largest city in the medieval world, built among granite boulders, looted and burned for six months in 1565 and never reoccupied.

name: Delphi
fact: The Greeks put the centre of the world on a mountainside above a fault, and the treasuries along the path up were each a city paying for its answer.

name: Mycenae
fact: Blocks of over 20 tonnes, some possibly near 100 — so large that later Greeks assumed one-eyed giants had done it.

name: Sassi di Matera
fact: A town where the street runs over the roof of the house below, cut into soft rock and lived in for nine thousand years — then evacuated in the 1950s as a national disgrace.

name: Kraków Old Town
fact: The walls came down and the moat became a park, so the ring is still there — as a green belt instead of a defence.

name: Bruges
fact: Preserved by its own failure: the channel that made it rich silted up around 1500, and a city with no trade builds nothing new over the old.

name: Kinderdijk
fact: Nineteen mills lifting water in stages, because draining peat makes it sink — so the more you drain, the further up you have to pump.

name: Nemrut Dağ
fact: A tomb under 49 m of loose gravel, because a heap that runs back into any hole you dig cannot be robbed.

name: Hattusa
fact: Burned about 1200 BC — and the fire baked its clay archive hard, which is why 30,000 tablets survived to be read.

name: Ephesus
fact: A great harbour city that is now three or four kilometres from the sea, because its own river filled the bay in.

name: Rock Carvings at Alta
fact: They were cut at the water’s edge, and the land has been rising ever since — so how high a panel sits tells you how old it is.

name: Roskilde Cathedral
fact: Eight hundred years of architecture in one building, because every Danish monarch since the 15th century wanted a chapel in it.

name: Speyer Cathedral
fact: The largest Romanesque church left standing, and its groin-vaulted nave is where a stone roof over a wide span stops being exceptional.

name: Serpent Mound
fact: 411 m of earth in the shape of a snake, with nobody buried in it — a picture meant to be seen from somewhere nobody could stand.

name: Ciudad Perdida
fact: 169 terraces cut into a mountainside, reached by 1,200 stone steps, and found again in 1972 by people looting it.

name: Pingyao
fact: A walled Ming town where Chinese banking began: Rishengchang moved silver on paper, and at its height handled almost half the country’s trade in it.

name: Luang Prabang
fact: A peninsula between two rivers with over thirty temples on it, and monks collecting alms along the same street every morning at sunrise.

name: Nelson's Dockyard
fact: A dockyard chosen for a hurricane: in September 1723 a storm wrecked 35 ships elsewhere and the ones in English Harbour were untouched.

name: Orion's Belt
fact: Three supergiants that only line up from here. An asterism is a coincidence of viewpoint, not a group of stars.

name: Nut (fastener)
fact: The same helix, cut into the wall of a hole instead of onto the outside of a bar.

name: Shaft (rotating)
fact: A bar held so it can only turn. Everything keyed to it turns at the same speed, which is the point and the constraint.

name: Fatehpur Sikri
fact: A capital built from nothing in 1571 and abandoned fourteen years later, because the water ran out.

name: Qutb Minar
fact: The tallest brick minaret in the world, tapering from 14.3 m at the base to 2.7 m at the top over 72.5 m.

name: Mahabodhi Temple
fact: One of the oldest brick buildings surviving in eastern India, standing beside a tree descended from the one the Buddha sat under.

name: Changdeokgung
fact: A palace laid out to fit the hill rather than the hill flattened to fit the palace — and a garden behind it with trees three centuries old.

name: Plain of Jars
fact: Over 2,100 stone jars, some 14 tonnes, hauled from a quarry eight kilometres away — and 80 million unexploded bomblets around them.

name: Wat Phra Kaew
fact: The king changes the Buddha’s gold garments three times a year, which is the clearest statement anywhere of what the temple is for.

name: Ningaloo Coast
fact: 260 km of fringing reef, in places less than 500 m from the beach — which is why you can swim out to a whale shark from the shore.

name: Tongariro National Park
fact: Given to the Crown in 1887 by a chief who wanted it protected, and the first place in the world listed as a cultural landscape for spiritual significance.

name: Shark Bay
fact: Water half as salty again as the sea, because the seagrass blocks the tide — and stromatolites growing in it, which is what life looked like for two billion years.

name: Rock Islands of Palau
fact: Limestone islands eaten away at the waterline by things that graze algae, so each one stands on a stalk.

name: Kīlauea
fact: Erupted continuously from January 1983 to September 2018 — one of the longest eruptions ever documented, and the home of Pele.

name: Lagoons of New Caledonia
fact: The longest continuous barrier reef in the world at 1,500 km, enclosing 24,000 km² of lagoon 25 m deep on average.

name: Willandra Lakes
fact: Dry lakes with crescent dunes on their eastern shores, holding the world’s oldest known cremation and 40,000 years of occupation.

name: Naracoorte Caves
fact: Animals fell into holes in the ground for over a million years, and the silt they landed in is 20 m deep.

name: Royal Exhibition Building
fact: Built in 1879–80 for an exhibition, and the first Parliament of Australia opened under its dome in 1901.

name: Papahānaumokuākea
fact: 1.5 million km² of ocean, ten islands and thirty submerged seamounts, and a quarter of its 7,000 species live nowhere else.

name: Langi of Lapaha
fact: Terraced tombs faced in slabs of coral rock that the sea made — sand compacted into 10 to 20 cm layers over centuries.

name: Galápagos Islands
fact: A hotspot chain 898 km off the mainland where the islands get older eastward — so the same lineage can be seen at several ages at once.

name: Potosí
fact: One mountain produced an estimated 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the 16th century, worked by 13,000 conscripted men a year.

name: Cradle of Humankind
fact: Dolomite caves that swallowed things and cemented them into breccia — Sterkfontein alone produced over a third of the early hominin fossils found before 2010.

name: Namib Sand Sea
fact: A desert that drinks fog. More than 180 days of it a year, made where a cold current meets warm air, and dunes over 300 m high made of river sand the sea gave back.

name: Tulum
fact: A walled Maya port on a 12 m cliff, with a shrine on top that seems to have been a beacon marking the one gap in the reef.

name: Classical Gardens of Suzhou
fact: Whole landscapes built at a size you can walk round in ten minutes, with the rocks chosen as the mountains.

name: Elmina Castle
fact: Put up by the Portuguese in 1482 — the oldest European building still standing south of the Sahara, and it was built for the gold before it was used for people.

name: Timgad
fact: A perfect Roman grid for 15,000 people, laid on empty ground about 100 AD — and then outgrown, so the city sprawls off its own plan in every direction.

name: Fes el Bali
fact: About 300 hectares of city with no cars in it — the streets are too narrow, so everything still moves by donkey.

name: Gedi Ruins
fact: A coral-stone Swahili town with drains and lavatories, abandoned by the mid-1600s, and nobody is sure why.

name: Blyde River Canyon
fact: A canyon 26 km long that is green rather than bare, with a 200 m waterfall depositing its own rock as it falls.

name: Ennedi Massif
fact: Sandstone towers and arches in the middle of the Sahara, with a waterhole in them holding crocodiles that shrank to fit.

name: Lake Chad
fact: Under two metres deep in most places, so a dry decade takes 95% of it — and a huge aquifer underneath is the reason anyone still lives there.

name: Songo Mnara
fact: Six mosques, four cemeteries and two dozen house blocks in rough coral and mortar, all built and abandoned inside three centuries.

name: Richtersveld
fact: 4,849 plant species in a desert, two in five of them found nowhere else — living on fog, in a landscape still herded by people in portable mat houses.

name: Redwood Forests
fact: The tallest trees on Earth take 40% of their water out of the air, and 96% of the old growth was cut down.

name: Ruins of Loropéni
fact: Six metres of laterite wall around 11,000 m², built on the gold road and abandoned in the early 19th century.

name: Salonga National Park
fact: 36,000 km² of rainforest with no roads in it — most of the park can only be reached by river, and parts have never been surveyed.

name: Quiriguá
fact: A small city that beheaded the king of a large one in 738, and then spent decades raising the biggest stelae anybody had ever cut.

name: Xochicalco
fact: A cave modified into an instrument: a shaft cut so that for three and a half months of the year the sun lands on the floor, and twice it lands straight down.

name: Willemstad
fact: Dutch gable houses on a Caribbean harbour, painted every colour but white.

name: Trinidad de Cuba
fact: Preserved by the collapse of the thing that built it: about 70 sugar mills in the valley behind, and no money to rebuild the town once they failed.

name: Blue and John Crow Mountains
fact: Country too steep and too wet to conquer, which is why the Windward Maroons held it — and why so much of what lives there lives nowhere else.

name: Kiyomizu-dera
fact: A veranda thrown out over a hillside on tall pillars, with no nails anywhere in it.

name: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
fact: 42 structures for one dead shogun, and a pagoda whose central pillar hangs from chains so an earthquake cannot break it.

name: Karakorum
fact: A Mongol capital with a silver tree in it that poured four drinks, built by a Parisian goldsmith taken as a slave.

name: Jiuzhaigou
fact: Lakes dammed by the rock their own water deposits, and coloured by what is dissolved in them.

name: Historic Vigan
fact: Stone below and timber above, with windows glazed in flattened oyster shell — a Chinese, Filipino and Spanish house all at once.

name: Komodo National Park
fact: About 5,100 of the largest lizard alive, on islands where nothing bigger ever arrived to argue.

name: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi
fact: Stopped when Timur died in 1405 and never finished — so the scaffolding is still in the front wall, and you can see how it was built.

name: Shahrisabz
fact: Two gate-towers 65 m high and nothing between them: Timur’s palace is a doorway with the building gone.

name: Nisa
fact: A Parthian fortress of mud brick, flattened by an earthquake — and the ivory drinking horns inside it are Greek in everything but who used them.

name: Kano City Walls
fact: Ten miles of clay wall thirty feet high, begun in the 11th century and finished in the 14th.

name: Struve Geodetic Arc
fact: 2,820 km of triangles from Norway to the Black Sea, measured between 1816 and 1855 to find the shape of the Earth — and they were within a fraction of a per cent.

name: Brunelleschi’s Dome
fact: 44 m across and built with no supporting frame — the first octagonal dome in history raised without one.

name: Venice
fact: Standing on alder trunks driven into mud, which do not rot because there is no oxygen down there to rot them.

name: Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba
fact: The columns were secondhand and too short, so a second tier of arches was put on top of the first to buy the height.

name: Akrotiri
fact: Three-storey houses with drains, buried in ash — and nobody in them. One gold object under a floor is all that was left behind.

name: Bryggen
fact: Timber warehouses that keep burning down and keep being rebuilt on the same foundations, so the plan is older than any of the boards.

name: Tower of London
fact: A Norman keep from 1078 wrapped in two later rings of wall and a 50 m moat — the castle grew outward around the tower rather than replacing it.

name: Khajuraho
fact: Sandstone cut to interlock and held down by nothing but its own weight — no mortar anywhere in it.

name: Lothal
fact: A basin 215 m long with a sluice in one wall, and forty years of argument about whether it is a dock.

name: Dambulla Cave Temple
fact: A groove cut along the overhang so rain drips clear of the opening — which is why 2,100 m² of painting is still on the ceiling.

name: Pashupatinath
fact: 518 small temples around one gilt-roofed pagoda on a river where the dead are burned — and the 2015 earthquake left the sanctum untouched.

name: Gunung Mulu
fact: A chamber 600 m long and 415 m wide inside a mountain, and three million bats coming out of the cave next door every evening.

name: Bosra
fact: A Roman theatre in black basalt that survives because somebody built a fortress around it and forgot to take it out.

name: Citadel of Aleppo
fact: A hill made by four thousand years of living on it, faced in limestone so nothing can climb the slope.

name: Old City of Sanaa
fact: 6,500 houses several storeys tall inside clay walls 9 to 14 m high — tower blocks built of earth.

name: Visby City Wall
fact: 3.44 km of the original 3.6 still standing, with 27 of 29 large towers — and the landward side was built first.

name: Edinburgh Old Town
fact: A street plan cut by a glacier: a volcanic crag with a tail of softer ground behind it, and everything built along the tail.

name: Roman Forum
fact: A marsh that had to be drained before anything could stand on it — and then it filled up again, with its own city washing down the hills.

name: Sintra
fact: A hill close enough to the Atlantic to make its own weather, planted with a forest and then built on.

name: Veliky Novgorod
fact: About a thousand letters written on birch bark by ordinary people, kept for eight centuries by wet ground that would not let them rot.

name: Danube Delta
fact: Probably 40% of it has been built in the last thousand years, out of what the river carried down.

name: Painted Churches of Bucovina
fact: Frescoes on the outside walls, where weather can get at them — which almost nobody else attempted, and which is why they are famous.

name: Orheiul Vechi
fact: A monastery cut into a limestone cliff inside a river bend that has been fortified by everyone who passed: Dacians, the Golden Horde, Moldavia.

name: Schönbrunn Palace
fact: 1,441 rooms, a folly on a 60 m hill closing the view, and a zoo in the garden that claims to be the oldest in the world.

name: Buda Castle
fact: Destroyed in the siege of 1686 and again in 1945, and rebuilt both times on the same hill in whatever style was current.

name: Konye-Urgench
fact: A 60 m minaret standing over a city that died twice — once by massacre and once because the river moved.

name: Jungfrau-Aletsch
fact: 23 km of glacier up to 900 m thick — the largest body of ice in the Alps, with a railway tunnelled up to look at it.

name: Vézelay Abbey
fact: A hill church that drew pilgrims for a relic and a crusade preached from it in 1146, and was rebuilt in the 19th century by Viollet-le-Duc.

name: Sigatoka Sand Dunes
fact: Dunes 20 to 60 m tall at a river mouth, with pottery over 2,600 years old and one of the largest burial grounds in the Pacific inside them.

name: Teouma
fact: The oldest known cemetery in the Pacific — and the skulls were taken off after burial and replaced with shell rings.

name: Pulemelei Mound
fact: 65 by 60 m of stacked basalt, the largest ancient structure in Samoa, and out of use by about 1800.

name: Lelu Ruins
fact: A walled town of about 1,500 people on a nearshore island, with burial pyramids for its nobility — abandoned about 1850.

name: Black Tea
fact: The trade calls it fermentation and nothing ferments: it is the leaf’s own enzyme oxidising the leaf, once the leaf is broken.

name: Fermented Cocoa
fact: Chocolate flavour is not in the bean. It is made in a heap of pulp over several days, and an unfermented bean tastes of raw potato.

name: Prune
fact: Only plums sweet enough not to ferment while they dry can be dried whole — which is why a prune is a particular kind of plum, not just a dried one.

name: Wind Slab
fact: Wind stacks snow on the sheltered side of a ridge faster than the snow underneath can settle to carry it. Slabs like this kill about nine in ten avalanche victims.

name: Hydroxymethylfurfural
fact: Absent from fresh food and made by heating sugar, so how much of it a honey holds says how warm it has been and for how long.

name: Blown Egg
fact: A shell emptied through two pinholes, which leaves the strongest shape a bird makes and none of its contents.

name: Wind Pollination
fact: Giving up on advertising: no scent, no petals, no nectar, and enormous numbers of grains small enough to stay up in moving air.

name: Resistant Starch
fact: Cooked starch that has been cooled recrystallises into a form the gut cannot digest — the same process that goes stale in bread.

name: Chocolate Bloom
fact: Cocoa butter finding a more stable crystal form and coming to the surface to do it. Ugly, harmless, and reversible by melting.

name: Bird Wing
fact: A forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna and a reduced fused hand, under asymmetric feathers. The same bones are in your arm.

name: Insect Wing
fact: Not a limb at all — a double sheet of the body wall stiffened by hollow veins, which is how an insect gets six legs and four wings both.

name: Enamel
fact: 96% mineral, the hardest tissue a body makes — and the only one with no living cells left in it, so it never heals.

name: Dentine
fact: The bulk of a tooth, under the enamel: bone-like, but threaded with tubules running to the nerve.

name: Tusk
fact: A tooth that never stops growing — which is exactly why it is worth killing for.

name: Bead
fact: The hole is the whole invention. Pierced shells 100,000 years old are among the oldest ornaments there are.

name: Necklace
fact: Beads on a cord — the oldest way of wearing a statement about yourself where other people can read it.

name: Dividers
fact: Two legs on a pivot. Fix one and swing the other and you have drawn every point the same distance from a centre — which is what a circle is.

name: Kaolin
fact: Weathered feldspar. It fires white and stays white, which almost no other clay does.

name: Porcelain
fact: Fired hot enough to turn partly to glass, so it rings, holds light through it, and takes no water at all.

name: Objective
fact: A state of the world you are not in yet, held in mind firmly enough to steer by. Everything that steers has one.

name: Yarn
fact: Fibre twisted until friction alone holds it together. Untwist it and it is dust again.

name: Strand
fact: Yarns twisted together, then twisted the other way when they become rope — which is what stops the whole thing unwinding.

name: Stave
fact: A shaped plank cut so its edges meet its neighbours at an angle, and only at that angle.

name: Hull
fact: The watertight shell. Everything else on a boat is cargo, rig or opinion.

name: Drumhead
fact: A membrane stretched until it will ring rather than thud.

name: Formwork
fact: The mould you build, fill, and then take away. The concrete keeps the shape and the marks.

name: Tumbler
fact: The part that blocks the bolt until it is lifted exactly far enough — no further.

name: Nock
fact: The notch that holds the arrow on the string until the string is faster than the fingers.

name: Fletching
fact: Feathers set slightly askew so the arrow spins, and a spinning arrow flies where it was pointed.

name: Sash
fact: The frame that holds the glass and slides, while the frame around it does not.

name: Croze
fact: The groove cut round the inside of a barrel's ends, and the tool that cuts it.

name: Cooper
fact: The trade that makes a watertight vessel out of dry flat wood and no fastenings at all.

name: Lacquer
fact: A finish that hardens by losing its solvent rather than by reacting — so it can always be softened again.

name: Mast
fact: A pole in compression, held up by ropes in tension. Take the ropes away and it falls.

name: Oar
fact: A lever whose fulcrum is the boat, not the water.

name: Oakum
fact: Old rope picked apart into loose fibre. Prisons and workhouses did the picking.

name: Caulk
fact: Fibre hammered into the seams until the wood cannot close and the water cannot open.

name: Clinker
fact: What limestone and clay become at 1,450 °C: grey nodules that will set hard again once ground and wetted.

name: Lead Came
fact: H-sectioned lead strip: the black lines in a stained-glass window are the structure, not the drawing.

name: Blank
fact: A disc of the right metal at exactly the right weight, with nothing on it yet.

name: Die (Tool)
fact: A hardened negative. Everything struck from it comes out the same — which is the whole point and the whole danger.

name: Bung
fact: A tapered plug in a tapered hole. The harder the pressure pushes, the tighter it seats.

name: Intrados
fact: The inner curve — the one you stand under and the one that cracks first.

name: Rubble Core
fact: The cheap middle between two good faces. Most of a thick wall is this.

name: Coping
fact: The hat on a wall. Without it, water gets into the top and takes the wall apart from inside.

name: Quoin
fact: The dressed stones at a corner, doing the job the rubble beside them cannot.

name: Excavation
fact: Taking ground away, and dealing with what the ground does once you have.

name: Ditch
fact: A trench dug to move water, or to stop somebody. Usually both.

name: Counterscarp
fact: The outer face of the ditch, and the one the defenders shoot along.

name: Berm
fact: A flat shelf between a ditch and the wall above it, so the wall does not slide into the hole.

name: Revetment
fact: A facing that holds earth back and stops it becoming a slope.

name: Causeway
fact: A raised way across ground that will not carry a road.

name: Subgrade
fact: The natural ground a road is built on. Everything above it exists because of how bad it is.

name: Sub-base
fact: Coarse stone between the ground and the road, spreading the load and draining the water.

name: Base Course
fact: The main structural layer of a road, and the one that fails last.

name: Binder Course
fact: The layer between the base and the surface, coarser than one and finer than the other.

name: Surface Course
fact: The layer that meets the tyre — chosen for grip and noise, not for strength.

name: Drainage
fact: Getting water off and out. Most things that fail structurally were drowned first.

name: Camber
fact: A road built deliberately out of level so that water runs off it.

name: Voussoir
fact: A wedge-shaped block. Cut the wedge right and an arch cannot fall in; cut it wrong and it cannot stand at all.

name: Course
fact: One horizontal layer. Getting the first one level decides every one above it.

name: Clay Lining
fact: Puddled clay — how a hole in the ground is made to hold water.

name: Keystone
fact: The last voussoir in, and the one that stops being needed the moment it is.

name: Springer
fact: The first voussoir, sitting where the curve leaves the vertical.

name: Impost
fact: The course an arch sits down on, projecting just enough to spread the load.

name: Extrados
fact: The outer curve of an arch — the side the load arrives on.

name: Haunch
fact: The shoulder of an arch, where the thrust tries hardest to escape.

name: Footing
fact: Wider than the wall on purpose, so the ground gets the load spread out.

name: Scarp
fact: The inner face of a defensive ditch — the one an attacker has to climb.

name: Breastplate
fact: A curved steel front. The curve is the armour — a flat plate of the same steel stops far less.

name: Backplate
fact: The other half of the cuirass, thinner — because a fleeing man is a smaller problem than a facing one.

name: Greave
fact: Shin armour, and the oldest piece of plate there is.

name: Buckle
fact: A frame, a pin and a hole. It has not changed in two thousand years because it did not need to.

name: Visor
fact: The part that has to come up, because a man who cannot breathe cannot fight.

name: Cheek Piece
fact: Hinged plates covering the jaw, and the reason a Roman helmet is recognisable at a glance.

name: Link
fact: One ring. A chain is only ever as strong as the worst of them.

name: Bucking Bar
fact: A heavy lump held against the far end, so the rivet upsets instead of just moving.

name: Leather Strap
fact: How armour, harness and almost everything else was held together before the buckle got cheap.

name: Pauldron
fact: Shoulder armour built from overlapping plates, so the arm still works.

name: Lame
fact: One strip in a stack of strips. The gaps between them are the joint.

name: Cuisse
fact: Thigh armour — the largest area a mounted man could not afford to leave open.

name: Chinstrap
fact: What keeps the helmet on the head it is meant to be on.

name: Liner
fact: The suspension inside a helmet. The shell does not touch your head, and that gap is the point.

name: Padding
fact: Layers of cloth, quilted. Soft armour that also stops hard armour from breaking you.

name: Nasal
fact: A single bar down the front of the face — the cheapest useful face protection there is.

name: Brow Reinforce
fact: An extra band across the front, where a downward cut actually lands.

name: Weld
fact: Two pieces of metal made into one, with no third thing holding them.

name: Bar Stock
fact: Metal in a plain useful shape, waiting to be something.

name: Swage
fact: A shaped die you hammer metal into, so every one comes out the same.

name: Hook
fact: A curve that holds as long as the load pulls the way you expected.

name: Shackle
fact: A U of metal with a removable pin, so two things can be joined and unjoined at will.

name: Rivet Set
fact: A cupped punch that forms the second head without flattening it.

name: Bore
fact: The hole, and the only dimension of a gun that really matters.

name: Touchhole
fact: A small hole at the breech, and the whole reason a cannon can be fired at all.

name: Trunnion
fact: Two stubs on the sides of a barrel, and the axis the whole gun turns about.

name: Breech
fact: The closed end. Everything the powder does, it does against this.

name: Muzzle
fact: The open end, and the last thing that touches the shot.

name: Rammer
fact: A staff with a head, for pushing everything down the bore in the right order and to the right depth.

name: Wadding
fact: Something soft rammed between powder and shot to hold each where it belongs.

name: Fleece
fact: One sheep's wool, taken off in a single piece.

name: Carding
fact: Pulling fibres straight and parallel, which is what makes them spinnable.

name: Batt
fact: A flat sheet of carded fibre, not yet twisted into anything.

name: Plain Weave
fact: Over one, under one. The simplest interlacing there is and the strongest for its weight.

name: Selvage
fact: The self-finished edge of woven cloth, where the weft turns round and goes back.

name: Sizing
fact: Stiffening a thread or a sheet so it survives the next process.

name: Grommet
fact: A metal ring in a hole, so the hole stops tearing.

name: Crucible
fact: A pot that stays solid at the temperature that melts whatever is inside it.

name: Float Glass
fact: Glass poured onto molten tin, which is flat because liquid is.

name: Lath
fact: Thin strips nailed with gaps, so wet plaster has something to grip.

name: Scratch Coat
fact: The first coat, deliberately scored so the second has something to bite on.

name: Float Coat
fact: The middle coat, which is where the wall is actually made flat.

name: Finish Coat
fact: Two or three millimetres of fine plaster, trowelled until it burnishes.

name: Brace
fact: A diagonal. A rectangle folds; a triangle does not.

name: Gusset
fact: A plate across a joint, so the joint is stronger than the members it joins.

name: Purlin
fact: A beam running along the roof, so the rafters can be lighter.

name: Eaves
fact: The overhang. It is what keeps rain off the wall you spent all that time building.

name: Lathe
fact: The machine that makes machines: it turns the work and holds the cutter still.

name: Boring Machine
fact: A cutter held rigid while the work turns — how a hole gets straighter than the thing making it.

name: Seam
fact: Where two pieces of cloth are joined, and where the garment will fail.

name: Hawk
fact: A square board with a handle underneath, holding the plaster the trowel takes from.

name: Shank
fact: The plain length between the working end and the end you hold.

name: Honing
fact: The last few microns, taken off with something finer than what shaped the edge.

name: Tempering
fact: Deliberately softening a quenched blade, because fully hard steel is glass.

name: Ferrule
fact: A ring at the end of a handle, stopping the wood from splitting when you hit it.

name: Grindstone
fact: A turning wheel of stone, taking metal off faster than any file.

name: Bolster
fact: The thickened collar between blade and handle, and the reason a knife balances.

name: Keyway
fact: The slot a key goes down, and the first thing that says no.

name: Escutcheon
fact: The plate round a keyhole. Half protection, half showing off.

name: Strike Plate
fact: The metal the bolt actually lands in, so the frame is not what takes the blow.

name: Linchpin
fact: A pin through the end of the axle. Take it out and the wheel comes off.

name: Journal
fact: The polished part of a shaft that actually runs in the bearing.

name: Axle Box
fact: The housing round the journal that holds the oil in and the grit out.

name: Web
fact: The thin vertical part of a beam, joining the two flanges that do the work.

name: Flange
fact: The wide part, out where the material does the most good.

name: Joist Hanger
fact: A pressed steel stirrup, so a joist can meet a beam without being cut into it.

name: Bevel
fact: An edge ground to an angle. The angle is the whole argument between sharp and durable.

name: Oxide Layer
fact: A film of glass grown out of the silicon itself, and the reason the transistor could be printed.

name: Photoresist
fact: A varnish that changes solubility where light hits it. The pattern is made by developing, not by cutting.

name: Photolithography
fact: Printing a circuit with light — millions of features at once, in one exposure.

name: Interconnect
fact: The wiring between transistors, which now takes more layers than the transistors do.

name: Lead Frame
fact: A stamped metal spider: the die sits at the middle and the legs become the pins.

name: Encapsulation
fact: The black plastic. Not decoration — the die will not survive air.

name: Junction
fact: Where n meets p, and current will go one way and not the other.

name: Emitter
fact: The terminal that supplies the carriers — doped hardest, because it has to win.

name: Collector
fact: The terminal that gathers what the emitter sent, and dissipates most of the heat.

name: Alnico
fact: Aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron. The strongest magnet there was, until the rare earths arrived.

name: Coercivity
fact: How hard it is to un-magnetise something. Low, and it is a transformer core; high, and it is a magnet.

name: Keeper
fact: A bar of soft iron across the poles, giving the field somewhere to go while the magnet is idle.

name: Winding
fact: Wire turned round a core enough times that a small current makes a large field.

name: Dielectric
fact: An insulator that stores energy by being pulled out of shape.

name: Getter
fact: A reactive metal flashed inside the envelope, to eat the gas the pump could not.

name: Fuse
fact: A wire chosen to fail, so that nothing more expensive does.

name: Filler
fact: Cheap inert powder in an expensive binder — and often what makes the mixture work.

name: Drier
fact: A metal salt that makes oil paint harden in a day instead of a month.

name: Stearin
fact: The hard fraction of a fat, and what turned the tallow candle into a decent one.

name: Panel
fact: A thin board held in a grooved frame, free to move as the wood changes size.

name: Stile
fact: The vertical member of a frame, running the full height and taking the hinges.

name: Threshold
fact: The board across the bottom of a doorway, and the oldest place in a house to leave an offering.

name: Bracket
fact: A right angle that turns a pulling load into a pushing one.

name: Transom
fact: The flat across a boat's stern — and the beam across the top of a window.

name: Housing
fact: The case: it keeps the mechanism aligned, and everything else out.

name: Laminations
fact: A core built from insulated sheets, so the currents that waste energy cannot circulate.

name: Magnetising Coil
fact: A brief, enormous current, to line the domains up once and for all.

name: Lead-in Wire
fact: The wire through the glass, which has to expand at exactly the rate the glass does.

name: Vitriol
fact: An old name for the sulfate salts, and the source of the oldest strong acid.

name: Gemstone
fact: A mineral chosen for hardness, rarity and what it does to light — in that order.

name: Setting
fact: How the stone is held. Every way of doing it trades light against security.

name: Circlet
fact: A plain band for the head. Every crown is one of these with things added.

name: Finial
fact: The ornament on top, where a structure has to stop.

name: Soldering
fact: Joining two metals with a third that melts lower than either.

name: Chasing
fact: Working metal from the front with punches, pushing it rather than cutting it.

name: Haft
fact: The handle, and the part that decides whether the tool is any good to use.

name: Hafting Resin
fact: Birch tar, pitch and beeswax — the oldest adhesive there is.

name: Arrowhead
fact: The business end, and the part archaeology actually finds.

name: Serration
fact: Teeth on an edge, so it saws where a plain edge would slide.

name: Splice
fact: Joining rope by weaving the strands into each other, not by tying.

name: Whipping
fact: Binding round the cut end so the rope cannot unlay itself.

name: Mortise and Tenon
fact: A tongue cut on one piece, a hole cut in the other. Seven thousand years old and still the joint everything else is measured against.

name: Gorée
fact: An island 900 m long off Dakar, held in turn by five European powers, and the memory of the Atlantic trade that ran through it.

name: Naqa
fact: A Kushite city with a Roman-looking kiosk beside an Egyptian temple beside a lion god nobody else had.

name: Osu Castle
fact: Danish, then British, then the seat of Ghana's government — a fort that never stopped being used.

name: Royal Court of Tiébélé
fact: Kassena earth houses painted by the women of the household, in patterns that are also the wall's maintenance.

name: Niokolo-Koba
fact: Where the Gambia river runs through Sudanian savanna — and the last West African lions outside Nigeria.

name: Dinosaur Provincial Park
fact: Badlands cut into a Cretaceous coastal plain, and more dinosaur species from one place than anywhere else.

name: Selous Game Reserve
fact: One of the largest protected areas in Africa, and largely one river's floodplain.

name: Humberstone Saltpeter Works
fact: A nitrate town in the driest desert on Earth, abandoned entire when synthetic ammonia made it worthless.

name: Ani
fact: The city of a thousand and one churches, emptied by an earthquake and a shifted trade route.

name: Pergamon
fact: A city built up a cone, with the steepest theatre in the ancient world and a library that made its own paper.

name: Hierapolis-Pamukkale
fact: A white terraced hillside made of the water's own dissolved limestone, with a Roman spa city on top.

name: Susa
fact: Occupied for five thousand years and capital to Elam, Persia and Parthia in turn.

name: Agra Fort
fact: Red sandstone walls 21 m high, and the room Shah Jahan was imprisoned in with a view of the Taj Mahal.

name: Elephanta Caves
fact: A temple with no walls built and no stone brought — cut downward and inward out of one basalt hill.

name: Jameh Mosque of Isfahan
fact: Twelve centuries of Iranian building in one courtyard — and the dome that invented the four-iwan plan.

name: Bhimbetka Rock Shelters
fact: Sandstone overhangs painted more or less continuously for perhaps thirty thousand years.

name: Mahabalipuram
fact: A Pallava port where the temples were carved out of the beach's own granite outcrops.

name: Great Living Chola Temples
fact: A 66 m granite tower whose capstone weighs 80 tonnes, on ground with no granite for 60 km.

name: Historic Centre of Macau
fact: Four centuries of Portugal and China on the same street, and a cathedral façade with nothing behind it.

name: Cave of Altamira
fact: Bison painted on the ceiling's own bulges, so the rock does the modelling — and nobody believed it for twenty years.

name: Vézère Valley Caves
fact: 147 sites and 25 decorated caves in one valley, including the one that named the Cro-Magnons.

name: Old City of Bern
fact: A medieval street plan that survived by being rebuilt in sandstone after the whole town burned.

name: Palaces and Parks of Potsdam
fact: Three centuries of Prussian building in one connected landscape, with terraced vines in front of the king's summer house.

name: Heart of Neolithic Orkney
fact: Skara Brae's neighbours: a chambered tomb aligned on midwinter, and two stone circles, all within a few miles.

name: Novodevichy Convent
fact: A fortified convent in a bend of the Moskva, used to hold inconvenient royal women.

name: Kotor
fact: A Venetian town at the head of a drowned river canyon, with 4.5 km of wall running up the mountain behind it.

name: Thatch
fact: Dry stems laid thick and steep. Water runs down the outside of each stalk and never reaches the inside.

name: Shirakawa-gō
fact: Roofs pitched at sixty degrees, because several metres of wet snow has to come off before it takes the house.

name: Kii Pilgrimage Routes
fact: Three shrine complexes joined by mountain paths, where kami and buddhas were treated as the same beings.

name: Pendant
fact: The thing that hangs. A necklace is what carries it, and usually the cheaper half.

name: Clasp
fact: The part that has to open, and therefore the part that fails.

name: Titans
fact: The generation before the Olympians, and the one they had to overthrow. Twelve children of Earth and Sky.

name: Volta Forts and Castles
fact: Around thirty forts on 500 km of coast, built by six European powers within sight of each other.

name: Bassari Country
fact: Terraced hill farming by three peoples who kept their own ways by living where nobody else wanted to be.

name: W-Arly-Pendjari
fact: One savanna held by three countries, and the last stronghold of the West African elephant and lion.

name: Rainforests of the Atsinanana
fact: Six parks on Madagascar's eastern scarp, holding species isolated for tens of millions of years.

name: Huascarán National Park
fact: The highest tropical range there is, and the deadliest avalanche ever recorded.

name: Kinabalu Park
fact: A granite dome still rising out of Borneo, with every band from lowland rainforest to bare rock on one slope.

name: Tràng An
fact: Tower karst carrying the sea's old notches, and caves lived in through the last glacial maximum.

name: Saryarka
fact: Steppe wetlands at the pinch point of a flyway, where a million birds have to pass the same lakes.

name: Hiraizumi
fact: A garden laid out as a working model of the Buddhist paradise, with the pond standing for the sea.

name: Fujian Tulou
fact: Rammed-earth rings up to five storeys, each holding a whole clan and shut with one door.

name: Manú National Park
fact: Cloud forest at 4,000 m down to Amazon lowland at 150, in one unbroken protected drop.

name: Portobelo–San Lorenzo
fact: The forts that guarded where all the silver of Peru left the Americas.

name: Hospicio Cabañas
fact: A single-storey hospice built round 23 courtyards so the sick could be wheeled everywhere, with Orozco's fire on the dome.

name: Historic Centre of Lima
fact: A viceregal capital that learned to build for earthquakes in cane and plaster instead of stone.

name: Pampulha Modern Ensemble
fact: The building that proved reinforced concrete could curve, and was refused consecration for fourteen years.

name: Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing
fact: Tombs sited by geomancy — mountain behind, water in front — and laid out so the approach is the architecture.

name: Koguryo Tombs
fact: Corbelled stone chambers with murals that are the best picture we have of daily life in early Korea.

name: Meiji Industrial Sites
fact: A country going from feudal to industrial in about fifty years, by copying and then improving.

name: Xanthos
fact: Pillar tombs cut as stone portraits of timber houses, by a people who twice burned their own city rather than yield it.

name: Sümela Monastery
fact: Built onto a ledge 300 m up a sheer face, with the rock itself as the back wall of the church.

name: Ahwar of Southern Iraq
fact: Reed marshes at the head of the Gulf, drained deliberately in the 1990s and partly refilled since 2003.

name: Westminster Abbey
fact: The tallest Gothic nave in England, and the building every English monarch since 1066 has been crowned in.

name: Dover Castle
fact: The key of England, with a Roman lighthouse in the bailey and tunnels dug under it in three different wars.

name: Jurassic Coast
fact: 185 million years of rock laid out along 154 km of shore, in order, tilted so you can walk through time.

name: Dacian Fortresses
fact: Six hill forts built in a masonry technique the Dacians invented and Rome destroyed with them.

name: Churches of Peace
fact: Timber-framed Lutheran churches built under conditions designed to make them impossible.

name: Tasmanian Wilderness
fact: A fifth of Tasmania, with rainforest that has been growing since Gondwana and rock art in limestone caves.

name: Wet Tropics of Queensland
fact: The oldest continuously surviving rainforest there is, still carrying the earliest flowering-plant lineages.

name: Byzantine Thessaloniki
fact: Fifteen churches spanning a thousand years, and the mosaics that show what was lost elsewhere to iconoclasm.

name: Arab-Norman Palermo
fact: Norman kings building with Arab craftsmen and Byzantine mosaicists, in one building at a time.

name: Venetian Works of Defence
fact: Low angled bastions built across three countries once cannon made high walls a liability.

name: Wooden Churches of Maramureș
fact: Oak churches with shingled spires up to 54 m, built without a nail because Orthodox congregations were barred from stone.

name: Wooden Churches of the Slovak Carpathians
fact: Roman Catholic, Protestant and Greek Catholic congregations, all solving the same problem in the same timber.

name: Wooden Churches of Southern Lesser Poland
fact: Gothic churches in horizontal log construction, by carpenters working from masonry drawings.

name: Ferapontov Monastery
fact: The only Dionisy fresco cycle that survives complete, painted in 34 days and never repainted.

name: Golden Mountains of Altai
fact: Where the steppe, the taiga and the desert meet, with frozen tombs that kept their contents intact.

name: Roman Monuments of Trier
fact: An imperial capital's basilica still standing to its full height, because it was turned into a church.

name: Roman and Romanesque Arles
fact: An amphitheatre that became a walled town with two hundred houses inside it, and was excavated back out.

name: Primeval Beech Forests
fact: One tree species retaking a continent after the ice, tracked across eighteen countries.

name: Lower German Limes
fact: A frontier that was a river, with forts along the bank and everything in the mud still there.

name: Shushtar Hydraulic System
fact: A Sassanid water system that cut a river in two, dropped it over mills, and irrigated 40,000 hectares.

name: Pattadakal
fact: Northern and southern temple styles built side by side, apparently as a deliberate comparison.

name: Hill Forts of Rajasthan
fact: Six forts on the Aravallis, each enclosing a town rather than a garrison.

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus
fact: A Victorian Gothic railway station with Indian craftsmen carving Indian detail into it.

name: Citadel of the Hồ Dynasty
fact: Limestone blocks up to 26 tonnes, dry-laid without mortar, for a dynasty that lasted seven years.

name: Baroque Churches of the Philippines
fact: Earthquake Baroque: buttresses so heavy the church looks like it is being held down.

name: Shirakami-Sanchi
fact: The last large stand of the beech forest that once covered northern Japan, never logged and with no roads.

name: Jōmon Sites of Northern Japan
fact: Ten thousand years of settled life without agriculture, which was supposed to be impossible.

name: Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks
fact: Four parks over one range, and the Burgess Shale inside them.

name: Pimachiowin Aki
fact: Boreal forest kept by Anishinaabeg who asked to be listed for how they live in it, not despite it.

name: Vega Archipelago
fact: A thousand years of people building houses for eider ducks and taking the down when they leave.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright Buildings
fact: Eight buildings across fifty years, including a house built over a waterfall and a museum that is one ramp.

name: Kluane–Wrangell–Glacier Bay
fact: The largest non-polar icefield on Earth, across two countries and four parks.

name: Islands of the Gulf of California
fact: A young sea made by a continent tearing, with deep water close inshore and 39% of the world's marine mammal species.

name: Cuban Coffee Plantations
fact: Terraced mountain estates built by French planters fleeing Haiti, worked by the people they brought with them.

name: Río Abiseo National Park
fact: Cloud forest that hid an entire city until 1985, and a monkey thought extinct for a century.

name: Jesuit Block of Córdoba
fact: A university, a church and five working farms run as one self-financing system.

name: Jesuit Missions of the Guaraní
fact: Mission towns of several thousand Guaraní each, planned around a square, and abandoned within a decade of the expulsion.

name: Ajina-Tepa
fact: A mudbrick monastery holding a 12-metre reclining Buddha, in a country now almost entirely Muslim.

name: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor
fact: A 866 km stretch of Silk Road with the caravanserais spaced by how far a camel walks in a day.

name: Letoon
fact: Three temples side by side and the trilingual stele that unlocked the Lycian language.

name: Sagalassos
fact: A city at 1,500 m, abandoned after an earthquake and never built over.

name: Colchic Rainforests and Wetlands
fact: Temperate rainforest that survived the ice ages when the rest of Europe's did not.

name: Landmarks of the Kingdom of Saba
fact: A dam that irrigated 25,000 acres for a thousand years, and whose failure is in the Quran.

name: Franciscan Missions of the Sierra Gorda
fact: Baroque façades carved by Otomí and Pame masons, who put their own iconography into the saints.

name: Akhsikath
fact: A Fergana capital famous for crucible steel, abandoned after an earthquake and then the Mongols.

name: Tusi Sites
fact: Chieftain seats where the empire ruled by appointing the people already in charge.

name: Sassanid Landscape of Fars
fact: A circular city and the dome on squinches that Byzantium and Islam both took from it.

name: Bahrain Pearling Trail
fact: Seventeen buildings, three oyster beds and one stretch of shore — an economy that ended in about five years.

name: Great Spa Towns of Europe
fact: Eleven towns built around mineral springs, and the shape of European leisure invented in them.

name: Leeds Castle
fact: A castle on two islands in its own lake, which is the moat and the defence and the reason it survived.

name: St James's Palace
fact: Still the sovereign's official seat, four hundred years after anyone lived in it full time.

name: Sacri Monti
fact: Nine hillsides of chapels with life-size painted figures, built as a pilgrimage for people who could not reach Jerusalem.

name: Medieval Monuments in Kosovo
fact: Byzantine and Romanesque built together, with fresco cycles that carried Balkan painting for 250 years.

name: Vineyard Landscape of Piedmont
fact: Hills where the soil changes every few hundred metres and the wine changes with it.

name: Classical Weimar
fact: A town of six thousand that held Goethe, Schiller and Herder at once, because a duchess collected them.

name: Thungyai–Huai Kha Khaeng
fact: The largest intact forest in mainland Southeast Asia, and a breeding tiger population still in it.

name: Dong Phayayen–Khao Yai
fact: A 230 km forest corridor kept whole so elephants can still walk the length of it.

name: Spillway
fact: The way water is meant to leave a dam, so it does not leave some other way.

name: Embankment
fact: An earth dam holds by weight and by not letting water through the middle.

name: Penstock
fact: The pipe that takes the head from the reservoir down to the turbine.

name: Caliper
fact: The clamp that squeezes the pads onto the disc.

name: Brake Fluid
fact: A liquid chosen because it will not compress and will not boil at the pedal.

name: Master Cylinder
fact: Where the foot's push becomes pressure in the line.

name: Retort
fact: A sealed vessel heated from outside, so what comes off can be caught.

name: Grate
fact: Bars with gaps, so air comes up through the fuel instead of round it.

name: Flue
fact: The passage that pulls the fire, by being taller than it is wide.

name: Scrubber
fact: Washing a flue gas before letting it out.

name: Heat Exchanger
fact: Two fluids swapping heat without ever touching.

name: Gyroscope
fact: A spinning mass that resists being turned, and says so.

name: Propellant
fact: Fuel and its own oxygen, so it burns where there is none.

name: Airframe
fact: The structure, with the engines and everything else taken off.

name: Spar
fact: The beam inside a wing, which is what actually stops it folding up.

name: Leaf Spring
fact: Steel strips stacked so the whole thing bends and rubs itself damped.

name: Steering
fact: Turning a wheel a lot so the road wheels turn a little, and feeling the road through it.

name: Tailgate
fact: The end of the bed that drops so things can be slid in.

name: Stucco
fact: Fine plaster that can be modelled, and holds the modelling.

name: Terrace
fact: Cutting a slope into steps so water walks instead of running.

name: Retaining Wall
fact: Holding earth back that would rather be a slope.

name: Arena
fact: The floor of the fight, sanded so it can be raked clean.

name: Podium
fact: The raised wall between the crowd and whatever is on the sand.

name: Vomitorium
fact: The passage that lets a full amphitheatre empty in minutes.

name: Awning
fact: Cloth on ropes over an open building, worked by sailors.

name: Basilica
fact: A long hall with aisles and a clerestory, built for business and then borrowed by the church.

name: Forum
fact: The open square everything civic faced onto.

name: Coolant
fact: A fluid whose whole job is to be somewhere else once it is hot.

name: Stela
fact: An upright slab, carved because somebody wanted it read later.

name: Paraffin Wax
fact: The wax almost every candle since the 1850s is made of, and it came out of a barrel of crude oil.

name: Soy Wax
fact: Soybean oil hardened by adding hydrogen, so a liquid becomes a solid that melts in the hand.

name: Polyester
fact: More clothing is made of this than of cotton, and it is made from oil.

name: Nylon
fact: The first fully synthetic fibre, and it went into parachutes before it went into stockings.

name: Viscose
fact: Wood pulp dissolved and squirted back out as a fibre — cellulose pretending to be silk.

name: Sunscreen
fact: Either it absorbs the ultraviolet or it reflects it, and the two work differently on the skin.

name: Shampoo
fact: A detergent mild enough for skin, plus everything added to undo what the detergent does.

name: Toothpaste
fact: An abrasive, a detergent, and the fluoride that is the only part that stops decay.

name: Skirt
fact: A tube or a cone of cloth, and one of the oldest cut garments there is.

name: Picture
fact: Any flat surface somebody has made stand for something else.

name: Cotton Plant
fact: A shrub that wraps its seeds in hair to float them away, and we take the hair.

name: Boll
fact: The capsule that splits open, and the moment the crop is ready.

name: Veneer
fact: Wood peeled off a log in one continuous sheet, like unrolling it.

name: Laminate
fact: Layers bonded so the stack has properties none of the layers has.

name: Creek
fact: A stream small enough to step over, and the thing every river is made of.

name: Rubbish
fact: What is left when a thing stops being worth keeping, which is a judgement rather than a property.

name: Litter
fact: Rubbish that was put down rather than thrown away.

name: Plywood
fact: Thin layers glued with the grain crossed, so it is strong both ways and cannot split.

name: Spaghetti
fact: Extruded rather than rolled, which is why it is round and why it is a machine's shape.

name: Risotto
fact: A rice that gives up its starch, stirred so the starch becomes the sauce.

name: Paella
fact: Cooked flat and never stirred, because the burnt layer at the bottom is the point.

name: Curry
fact: A word the British applied to several hundred unrelated dishes, and which stuck.

name: Pie
fact: Pastry as a container first and a food second — the crust was originally the pot.

name: Dumpling
fact: Dough round a filling — found independently almost everywhere people had both.

name: Porridge
fact: Grain and water cooked until the starch bursts. Probably the oldest cooked dish there is.

name: Casserole
fact: One dish, in the oven, for long enough that tough things become tender.

name: Static Electricity
fact: Charge that has nowhere to go, until suddenly it does.

name: Circuit
fact: A loop. Break it anywhere and nothing anywhere in it works.

name: Buoyancy
fact: The water pushes up by exactly the weight of the water that is not there any more.

name: Density
fact: How much of a thing is in the space it takes up.

name: Viscosity
fact: How much a fluid objects to being sheared.

name: Surface Tension
fact: A liquid's surface behaving like a skin, because the molecules underneath pull and the ones above do not.

name: Capillary Action
fact: Water climbing a narrow tube against gravity, and the reason a wick works.

name: Conduction
fact: Heat passing through a solid by jostling, without anything moving from one end to the other.

name: Convection
fact: Hot fluid rises because it is less dense, and something colder comes in behind it.

name: Reflection
fact: Light bouncing at the angle it arrived, or scattering if the surface is rough.

name: Refraction
fact: Light bending because it travels slower in one thing than another.

name: Resonance
fact: Pushing something at the rate it already wants to move, so small pushes get large.

name: Wok
fact: A bowl of thin steel, so the bottom is fierce and the sides are not.

name: Charge
fact: The property that makes things pull and push without touching.

name: Stir Fry
fact: Very hot metal, very little time, and everything cut to cook at the same rate.

name: Voltage
fact: The push. Not how much charge, but how badly it wants to move.

name: Acrylic Fibre
fact: The synthetic that was made to be wool, and is warm for the same reason.

name: Spandex
fact: A fibre that stretches to five times its length and goes back.

name: Polypropylene
fact: The lightest common plastic — it floats — and the one with the living hinge.

name: Epoxy
fact: Two liquids that become a solid by reacting with each other rather than by drying.

name: Carbon Fibre
fact: Filaments of nearly pure carbon, stiffer than steel for their weight and brittle without warning.

name: Fibreglass
fact: Glass drawn fine enough to bend without breaking.

name: Chipboard
fact: Wood chips and glue pressed into a board, using what the sawmill would have burnt.

name: Vinyl
fact: The plastic that was flooring, then records, then flooring again.

name: Neoprene
fact: A synthetic rubber full of nitrogen bubbles, which is what makes a wetsuit work.

name: Deodorant
fact: It does not stop sweat smelling. It stops the bacteria that make the smell.

name: Moisturiser
fact: Mostly it does not add water. It stops water leaving.

name: Spectacles
fact: Two lenses at the right distance, and the frame is the hard part.

name: Wheelchair
fact: A chair the user drives, which is a different machine from one they are pushed in.

name: Crutch
fact: Moving load off a leg and into the arms and shoulders.

name: Prosthesis
fact: Replacing a part, and the difficult end is where it meets what is left.

name: Painkiller
fact: Blocking the signal, or blocking the chemistry that makes the signal.

name: Plaster Cast
fact: Holding two ends of a bone still for long enough that they knit.

name: Spinneret
fact: A plate of fine holes. Everything synthetic that is a fibre came out of one.

name: Rayon
fact: The first manufactured fibre, and it is made of trees.

name: Kevlar
fact: Chains lined up so straight that the fibre beats steel by weight.

name: Stream
fact: Water gathered into a channel it cut itself.

name: Brook
fact: The smallest named running water, and mostly a matter of local usage.

name: Pond
fact: Still water shallow enough that light reaches the bottom everywhere.

name: Puddle
fact: Water that cannot soak in and has nowhere to run.

name: Culvert
fact: A pipe that lets a stream cross under a road instead of over it.

name: Watershed
fact: The line where a raindrop's whole future is decided.

name: Runoff
fact: The rain that does not soak in, and it carries whatever it crosses.

name: Oxbow
fact: A meander that got cut off, left as a lake shaped like the bend it used to be.

name: Wiring
fact: Conductors sized for the current they will carry and insulated for the voltage.

name: Wallpaper
fact: Printed paper hung on a wall, and the first mass-produced interior decoration.

name: Shower
fact: Water broken into a spray so a little of it wets all of you.

name: Bath
fact: A vessel large enough to sit in, which is a lot of hot water.

name: Fridge
fact: Moving heat out of a box, which takes work, which is why the back is warm.

name: Washing Machine
fact: Agitation, detergent, temperature and time — and you can trade any one against the others.

name: Plumbing
fact: Water in under pressure, out under gravity, and the two never meeting.

name: Furniture
fact: The movable things that make a room usable, and the joints are the whole craft.

name: Pottery
fact: Clay made permanent by fire, and the most abundant thing archaeology has.

name: Windmill
fact: Sails, a shaft, and a way of turning the whole thing to face whatever the wind is doing.

name: Mine
fact: A hole dug at a thing worth more than the digging, and the water is always the problem.

name: Smithy
fact: A forge, an anvil, water, and a floor that will not burn.

name: Bakery
fact: An oven big enough to be worth heating, which is why it was communal before it was commercial.

name: Tannery
fact: Put downwind and downstream of everywhere, for good reason.

name: Bank
fact: Somewhere to leave money, which works only because not everyone asks for it at once.

name: Garden
fact: Ground kept deliberately, which is the only thing every garden has in common.

name: Glassmaking
fact: Sand melted with something to lower its melting point and something to stop it dissolving.

name: Papermaking
fact: Fibre suspended in water and lifted out on a screen, so it mats as it drains.

name: Cheesemaking
fact: Separating milk into curd and whey, and then deciding what to do with the curd.

name: Kitchen
fact: Fire, water and a surface, arranged so one person can reach all three.

name: Camera
fact: A dark box with a hole, and everything since has been about controlling the hole.

name: Watermill
fact: A wheel in a stream, and the whole medieval economy hung off it.

name: Extruder
fact: A screw in a heated barrel, pushing a melt through a hole in a shape.

name: Fastener
fact: Anything that holds two things together and can be taken apart again.

name: Additive
fact: A few per cent of something else, doing most of the work.

name: Mount
fact: Where a thing is attached, and where its vibration goes next.

name: Initiator
fact: The molecule that starts a chain reaction and is consumed doing it.

name: Adhesive
fact: Sticking is two different problems: wetting the surface, and then setting.

name: Gasket
fact: Something soft between two hard things, squashed until the gap is gone.

name: Bush
